shang-dynasty.name: Shang dynasty
shang-dynasty.summary: A Chinese royal dynasty that ruled the Yellow River valley in the 2nd millennium BCE, the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by archaeology, known for oracle-bone writing found at its capital near Anyang.

gansu.name: Gansu
gansu.summary: A province in northwestern China straddling the Tibetan and Loess plateaus, through which the ancient Northern Silk Road ran via the Hexi Corridor.

qinghai.name: Qinghai
qinghai.summary: Inland province in Northwestern China on the Tibetan Plateau, named after Qinghai Lake, China's largest lake.

ordos-plateau.name: Ordos Plateau
ordos-plateau.summary: A highland sedimentary basin in northern China enclosed by a bend of the Yellow River, China's second-largest sedimentary basin.

huangjiu.name: Huangjiu
huangjiu.summary: A type of Chinese rice wine, typically light yellow to brown, brewed from steamed grains and fermented for weeks, popular in East China.

xia-dynasty.name: Xia dynasty
xia-dynasty.summary: Traditionally China's first dynasty, said to be founded by Yu the Great; its historicity is debated, with many Chinese archaeologists linking it to the Erlitou culture (c. 1900-1500 BC).

yangshao-culture.name: Yangshao culture
yangshao-culture.summary: A Neolithic culture along the middle Yellow River in China, roughly 5000 to 3000 BC, marked by advances in agriculture, architecture, and crafts.

longshan-culture.name: Longshan culture
longshan-culture.summary: A late Neolithic culture in the Yellow River valley of northern China, from about 3000 to 1900 BC, noted for its polished black pottery.

zhou-dynasty.name: Zhou dynasty
zhou-dynasty.summary: A Chinese royal dynasty that ruled for 790 years, roughly 1046 to 256 BC, the longest of any Chinese dynasty, its power fading before Qin conquered it.

guang-vessel.name: Guang
guang-vessel.summary: A bronze ritual wine vessel from China's Shang and Zhou dynasties (about 1700-900 BCE), used to pour rice wine at banquets and often placed in high-status burials.

taotie.name: Taotie
taotie.summary: An ancient Chinese mythological creature commonly shown as a mask-like motif on bronze ritual vessels during the Shang and Zhou dynasties.

bi-jade.name: Bi
bi-jade.summary: A circular ancient Chinese jade artifact, first produced in the Neolithic Liangzhu culture (3400 to 2250 BCE) and later mainly during the Shang, Zhou and Han dynasties.

liangzhu-culture.name: Liangzhu culture
liangzhu-culture.summary: A Chinese Neolithic culture (3300–2300 BC) in the Yangtze River Delta, marked by jade, silk and lacquer elite burials and considered one of China's earliest state societies.

chinese-jade.name: Six Ritual Jades
chinese-jade.summary: Six jade shapes—the bi, cong, huang, hu, gui and zhang—first found in the 3rd-millennium BCE Liangzhu culture, later interpreted by the Rites of Zhou as representing the sky, earth and four directions.

rites-of-zhou.name: Rites of Zhou
rites-of-zhou.summary: An ancient Chinese text on bureaucracy and government organization, later grouped with the Book of Rites as one of Confucianism's 'Three Rites'. It likely reflects Warring States-era administrative reforms rather than the earlier Zhou dynasty.

taosi.name: Taosi
taosi.summary: An archaeological site in Shanxi, China, representing the late phase of the Longshan culture, from 2300 to 1900 BC.

erlitou.name: Erlitou
erlitou.summary: A Chinese archaeological site in Henan, occupied from around 1860 BC, that became a major early Bronze Age city and centre of bronze casting.

robert-bagley.name: Robert Bagley
robert-bagley.summary: American sinologist and professor of Chinese art history and archaeology at Princeton University.

late-shang.name: Late Shang
late-shang.summary: The final period of China's Shang dynasty, from the 13th to mid-11th century BC, known for oracle bone writing and centered on the capital at Yinxu near Anyang.

deer-stones-culture.name: Deer stones
deer-stones-culture.summary: Bronze Age megaliths carved with images of flying deer, found mainly in Mongolia and nearby Siberia, generally placed near ancient graves and thought to guard the dead.

oracle-bone.name: Oracle bones
oracle-bone.summary: Ox shoulder bones and turtle shells used for divination in Late Shang China, around 1250 to 1050 BCE, inscribed with questions to deities and bearing the earliest known substantial body of Chinese writing.

erligang-culture.name: Erligang culture
erligang-culture.summary: A Bronze Age urban culture in China, roughly 1600–1400 BC, named for the site where the primary settlement, Zhengzhou Shang City, was found in 1951.

zhengzhou.name: Zhengzhou
zhengzhou.summary: Capital of Henan Province, China, a cradle of Chinese civilization and site of an early Shang dynasty capital with a rammed-earth walled city dating to about 1600 BC.

xi-zhong.name: Xi Zhong
xi-zhong.summary: Legendary Xia dynasty minister traditionally credited with inventing the chariot in the 2nd millennium BC, though archaeology instead places chariot use closer to 1200 BC.

anyang.name: Anyang
anyang.summary: A city in Henan, China, and site of the ancient capital of Yin, the first stable capital of the Shang dynasty and one of the birthplaces of Chinese civilization.

tomb-of-fu-hao.name: Tomb of Fu Hao
tomb-of-fu-hao.summary: A Shang dynasty royal tomb near Anyang, China, discovered intact in 1976, holding bronze vessels naming Fu Hao, a military leader and consort of King Wu Ding around 1200 BCE.

fu-hao.name: Fu Hao
fu-hao.summary: Shang dynasty military general, high priestess and wife of King Wu Ding, who died around 1200 BC; her intact tomb, found in 1976, is the main source on her life.

wu-ding.name: Wu Ding
wu-ding.summary: King of the Shang dynasty who died around 1192 BC; oracle bone inscriptions from his reign, unearthed in 1899, are the earliest confirmed Chinese writing and make up over half of all known Shang inscriptions.

yinxu.name: Yinxu
yinxu.summary: Archaeological site of Yin, the final Shang dynasty capital (c. 1250–1046 BCE), where oracle bone script was found; rediscovered in 1899 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006.

erlitou-culture.name: Erlitou culture
erlitou-culture.summary: An early Bronze Age archaeological culture in the Yellow River valley, dated to roughly 1750–1500 BC, considered by most archaeologists to be China's first state-level society.

sima-qian.name: Sima Qian
sima-qian.summary: Chinese historian of the early Han dynasty, c. 145–86 BC, considered the father of Chinese historiography for the Shiji, spanning over two thousand years of history.

bamboo-annals.name: Bamboo Annals
bamboo-annals.summary: A chronicle of ancient China running from legendary times to 299 BC, focused later on the State of Wei, surviving today in two disputed versions after the original was possibly lost.

oracle-bone-script.name: Oracle bone script
oracle-bone-script.summary: Oldest known form of written Chinese, carved into bones and shells to record royal divinations for the Late Shang court; most surviving examples come from the last Shang capital near modern Anyang.

shiji.name: Shiji
shiji.summary: A Chinese historical text written in the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BC by Han dynasty historian Sima Qian, covering 2,500 years of history and setting the model for all later Chinese dynastic histories.

yu-the-great.name: Yu the Great
yu-the-great.summary: A legendary Chinese sage-king credited with controlling great floods and founding the Xia dynasty, though no contemporary evidence confirms he existed.

du-kang.name: Du Kang
du-kang.summary: A legendary figure in Chinese tradition credited with inventing alcoholic drink and later worshipped as patron deity of winemakers in China and Japan; whether he really lived is unknown.

twenty-eight-mansions.name: Twenty-Eight Mansions
twenty-eight-mansions.summary: A system of Chinese constellations tracking the Moon's path across the sky roughly one mansion per day, also used in Japan and paralleled by India's nakshatra system.

majiayao-culture.name: Majiayao culture
majiayao-culture.summary: Neolithic culture (3300 to 2000 BC) of China's upper Yellow River region, notable for pioneering agricultural settlement there and for finely painted pottery.

seima-turbino-culture.name: Seima-Turbino culture
seima-turbino-culture.summary: A pattern of Bronze Age burial sites across northern Eurasia sharing similar bronze artifacts, linked to nomadic warrior-metalworkers who traveled on horseback or two-wheeled carts, dated to about 2200 to 1900 BCE.

palaeoloxodon.name: Palaeoloxodon
palaeoloxodon.summary: An extinct elephant genus that spread from Africa into Eurasia, including some of the largest land mammals ever known and, on Mediterranean islands, some of the smallest elephants.

gaocheng-shijiazhuang.name: Gaocheng
gaocheng-shijiazhuang.summary: A district of Shijiazhuang city in China's Hebei province, on the upper reaches of the Hutuo River.

shijiazhuang.name: Shijiazhuang
shijiazhuang.summary: Capital and most populous city of China's Hebei province, southwest of Beijing, with over 11 million residents as of the 2020 census.

hebei.name: Hebei
hebei.summary: A province in North China surrounding Beijing and Tianjin, home to over 75 million people and historic sites including a section of the Great Wall.

qijia-culture.name: Qijia culture
qijia-culture.summary: An early Bronze Age culture (2400 to 1600 BC) centred around the upper Yellow River in Gansu and Qinghai, China, regarded as one of the country's earliest bronze-using cultures.

warring-states-period.name: Warring States period
warring-states-period.summary: A Chinese era from about 475 to 221 BC marked by intense warfare and political consolidation, ending when the state of Qin conquered its rivals and founded the first imperial dynasty.

guifang.name: Guifang
guifang.summary: An ancient northern people who fought the Shang dynasty (1600–1046 BCE); the Chinese name combines words meaning 'ghost' and 'border country.'

victoria-herridge.name: Victoria Herridge
victoria-herridge.summary: British palaeontologist and co-founder of TrowelBlazers who has written on island mammal evolution, mammoth cloning ethics, and women's history in science.

siwa-culture.name: Siwa culture
siwa-culture.summary: A Bronze Age culture, about 1350 to 650 BCE, in southeast Gansu, China, discovered in 1924 and known for pottery with saddle-shaped mouths.

tianxia.name: Tianxia
tianxia.summary: A Chinese concept meaning 'all under Heaven', denoting the world or realm divinely appointed to the Chinese sovereign, central to classical ideas of order.

jie-of-xia.name: Jie of Xia
jie-of-xia.summary: Jie of Xia: Traditionally the last, tyrannical ruler of China's Xia dynasty (traditionally dated c. 1728–1675 BCE), whose defeat by Tang of Shang around 1600 BCE ended the dynasty.

tang-of-shang.name: Tang of Shang
tang-of-shang.summary: First king of the Shang dynasty (c. 1670–1587 BC), traditionally seen as a virtuous ruler who overthrew Jie, the last king of the Xia dynasty.

xia-shang-zhou-chronology-project.name: Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project
xia-shang-zhou-chronology-project.summary: A 1996 Chinese government project using radiocarbon dating, archaeology, texts and astronomy to date the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties, dating the Xia's start to about 2070 BCE, though some scholars dispute its conclusions.

liu-xin-scholar.name: Liu Xin
liu-xin-scholar.summary: A Chinese astronomer, classicist, imperial librarian, mathematician and politician of the Western Han and Xin dynasties (c. 46 BCE-23 CE), son of librarian Liu Xiang.

shangdi.name: Shangdi
shangdi.summary: The name for the Chinese "Lord Above," the highest deity in classical Chinese theology, rooted in Shang-dynasty worship and still used today in several Chinese religious and philosophical traditions.

qi-of-xia.name: Qi of Xia
qi-of-xia.summary: Second sovereign of the Xia dynasty and son of Yu the Great, who ruled for roughly nine to ten years.

li-zehou.name: Li Zehou
li-zehou.summary: Chinese scholar of philosophy and intellectual history (1930–2021), influential in aesthetics and the 1980s Chinese New Enlightenment.

david-keightley.name: David Keightley
david-keightley.summary: An American sinologist (1932–2017) and Berkeley professor whose studies of Chinese oracle bones reshaped scholarly understanding of Shang dynasty history.

lanzhou.name: Lanzhou
lanzhou.summary: Capital of Gansu province in northwestern China, on the Yellow River, historically a major link on the Northern Silk Road.

niuheliang.name: Niuheliang
niuheliang.summary: A Neolithic archaeological site in Liaoning, Northeast China, belonging to the Hongshan culture (4700-2900 BC), where a temple, altar and cairn were discovered in 1983.

guo-dashun.name: Guo Dashun
guo-dashun.summary: A Chinese archaeologist, born 1938, known for excavating the Hongshan culture site at Niuheliang and for theories that helped reshape understanding of early Chinese civilisation.

hongshan-culture.name: Hongshan culture
hongshan-culture.summary: A Neolithic culture of northeast China's West Liao river basin, dated about 4700 to 2900 BC, named after a site discovered in 1908 and excavated in 1935.

dagger-axe.name: Dagger-axe (ge)
dagger-axe.summary: A Chinese polearm with a dagger-shaped blade mounted on a perpendicular shaft, used from the Longshan culture to the Han dynasty; first made of stone, later bronze or ceremonial jade.

houmuwu-ding.name: Houmuwu Ding
houmuwu-ding.summary: A rectangular bronze ritual vessel of China's Shang dynasty, the heaviest surviving bronze from the ancient world, unearthed in 1939 near the last Shang capital at Anyang.
